newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Iraqi official says country remains "resolute".
newsitem.headline: Iraqi official says country remains "resolute".

text.p: An Iraqi foreign ministry official on Wednesday described the current mood of the Baghdad government as "resolute" rather than "defiant" in the face of further threatened American air strikes.
Riyadh al-Qaysi, an undersecretary in the foreign ministry, was asked by reporters if Iraq was defiant and intended to escalate confrontations with the United States.
"Defiant?" he said. "I would say resolute. You have to gauge the popular sentiment on this. We are resolute on this."

Al-Qaysi maintained that any flight ban over Iraq was illegal and not sanctioned by the United Nations. He said again that Iraq had moved into its northern territory at the request of a Kurdish group.

The United States retaliated with cruise missile strikes last week when Iraqi troops moved into the northern sector to aid forces of Kurdish leader Masood Barzani fight forces loyal to rival Kurdish leader Jalal Talabani.
Apparently unfazed by U.S. air strikes, Iraq fired a missile at U.S. warplanes over northern Iraq on Wednesday, prompting fresh warnings from the Pentagon.

"If you train radar on our aircraft, I am performing self-defense against an act that is unlawful," he said. "There is no such thing as a no-fly zone. It is illegal. Otherwsie you have the law of the jungle."
"We have threatened no one," he continued. "Who is escalating? Is it Iraq or the United States. This whole crisis was imposed by the United States... Enough is enough."
Iraq's foreign minister, Mohammed Saeed al-Sahaf, in a letter to the United Nations on Wednesday said that U.S. flights over Iraqi territory were tantamount to military aggression.

Al-Qaysi had earlier planned a visit to New York to speak to Rolf Ekeus, the chairman of the U.N. Special Commission in charge of ridding Iraq of weapons of mass destruction. Blanket trade sanctions against Baghdad cannot be lifted until Ekeus has accounted for all of Iraq's dangerous weapons potential.
He gave no details on what had been achieved except to say "my mission here in New York really is very much in support of the continuation of our work."
Ekeus had stopped flying surveillance helicopters over Iraq and in areas where U.S. missiles might be fired. He said on Wednesday most of the flights had resumed again.
Al-Qaysi maintained that the United States alone had prevented sanctions from being lifted because of "sheer aggressive power" in imposing its will.
He said he would speak to all Security Council members individually, except for the United States and Britain, and would probably also meet Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali.

The secretary-general has put on hold an oil-for-food deal that is an exemption to the sanctions. This plan would allow Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to purchase badly needed food and other supplies for its civilians.
Asked if he thought the plan would be implemented, al-Qaysi said: "It must be implemented. The Security Council has to implement its own word and commitments."
He said he knew of no U.N. request to change any part of the plan because of the new crisis in the Kurdish north.
